beats.say: When people worry about where computer chips come from, they look here. At Taiwan.
One industry study, using twenty-nineteen data, found about ninety percent of the world's most advanced chip-making capacity on this one island.
But turn the globe almost thirteen thousand kilometres, to a small town in the mountains of North Carolina.
This is Spruce Pine. About two thousand two hundred people live here.
On the hills around it, two companies dig up a rock that the chip industry has found very hard to replace.
In September twenty twenty-four, a hurricane buried these mountains in rain. Both companies stopped work.
Chip sales last year came to nearly eight hundred billion dollars.
So why does all of that lean on one small town? And what happened when the town went dark?
To answer that, forget the chip for a moment. We need to talk about a bowl.
A chip starts as rock. Ordinary quartz rock is turned into silicon, and the silicon is cleaned until it is almost perfectly pure. Then comes the hard part.
A chip needs its silicon as one single crystal. Every atom in line, like tiles on a floor, with almost none out of place.

The trick for growing one goes back to a Polish chemist, Jan Czochralski. The story goes that one evening he dipped his pen into molten tin instead of ink. When he lifted it, a thin thread of metal came up with it: a single crystal. He published the method in nineteen eighteen.
Chip makers still use his idea. They fill a bowl with chunks of pure silicon, and heat it past fourteen hundred degrees Celsius, until it melts.
They dip a tiny seed crystal into the melt.
Then they pull it up, very slowly, turning it as it rises. A large crystal grows from the thin seed.
The finished crystal is called an ingot. One quartz producer, describing how wafers are made, says a full ingot can weigh over five hundred kilograms and measure more than four metres.
The ingot is sliced into thin discs called wafers, each about a millimetre thick.
And chips are built on the wafers. The same company says one three-hundred-millimetre ingot can make about two million chips.
Now look again at the bowl.
It is called a crucible, and it has a terrible job. It must hold liquid silicon, at extreme heat, for hundreds of hours.
The crystal has to come out pure and uniform. So the bowl that holds the melt has to be extremely pure too.
So the bowl must take the heat, and stay pure. The answer is quartz: melted, and shaped into a bowl.
And not just any quartz. The Geological Survey says the purest products have fewer than ten parts in every million of anything else.
And each bowl has a working life. That producer says one crucible pulls about eight ingots, over four hundred hours.
So here is the first surprise. The famous quartz is not inside your phone's chips. It is the bowl they were born in.
Ordinary quartz is good enough to make the silicon. But quartz pure enough for the bowl is found in only a few places on Earth.
The best known of them is here, in the Blue Ridge mountains, around Spruce Pine.
One company says this district was made about three hundred and eighty million years ago, when Africa collided with North America. Dating of the rocks gives a similar age.
Deep underneath, molten rock was trapped. One company says it cooled slowly. The other says there was very little water around to carry impurities in.
Whichever it was, the result is a rock holding quartz of rare purity.
The United States Geological Survey puts it at more than ninety-nine point nine nine nine percent pure.
China has announced large reserves of its own. In China's first tests, as the survey reports them, the purity came in just below Spruce Pine's.
Two companies produce this quartz here. Sibelco, which sells it under the name Iota. And The Quartz Corp.
The Geological Survey says that in twenty twenty-five, two companies produced it in the United States, both around Spruce Pine. And for most uses, it says, there is no economic substitute.
You will often hear that seventy to ninety percent of the world's supply comes from this one town. We went looking for where that number comes from.
We could not find it in any primary source we read. The survey says world production figures are simply not available. It only estimates that the United States leads.
Here are numbers that are official. All the silicon wafers sold last year earned about eleven billion dollars. The chips built on them, nearly eight hundred billion.
And the pure quartz? Take the survey's rounded estimate of tonnes sold, at its very top price, and America's whole supply comes to roughly a billion dollars a year. A speck, holding up a giant.
In November two thousand eight, a fire broke out at one of the plants here. Investigators found no sign of foul play, and recorded the cause as undetermined.
On the night of the twenty-sixth of September, twenty twenty-four, Hurricane Helene came ashore in Florida as a category four storm, and drove north.
In Spruce Pine, both quartz companies had stopped work by the twenty-sixth. The Quartz Corp says it stopped in preparation.
Then the rain came. Gauges six or seven miles from the town measured between twenty-three and twenty-four inches. That is about sixty centimetres of water.
Some rivers and creeks in the county rose to their highest levels in recorded history. Roads and bridges washed out. The power failed.
In the south of this one county: more than two hundred landslides. An estimated hundred thousand trees down. And one person drowned in the river that runs through the valley.
And the railway that follows the river north, through a narrow gorge into Tennessee, was torn apart.
Far away, the question was simple. Was the quartz gone?
A week later, Sibelco reported its first look at the plants. They had, in its words, only sustained minor damage.
The Quartz Corp said its damage was mostly around side units. Later it said up to a quarter of its workers were out helping the town recover.
About two weeks after the storm, Sibelco said production and shipments had restarted. By late October, The Quartz Corp said its plants were gradually restarting too.
And the companies said there were stocks. The Quartz Corp pointed to safety stocks along the chain, and to raw material held in Norway.
So, by the companies' own accounts, the plants had largely survived. What broke was everything around them.
About sixty miles of that railway were badly damaged. In the gorge, the track had to be built again, mile by mile.
You may hear that Spruce Pine was cut off from trains for a whole year. The railway's own notice says limited service north of the town began in the middle of January.
But the gorge took far longer. The whole line returned to service on the twenty-fifth of September, twenty twenty-five. Almost exactly one year.
The railway's own filings put the cost at about five hundred and twenty million dollars.
A year after the storm, trains ran the whole line again.
So was the world lucky? Partly. The storm stopped the quartz for weeks, not for years.
But look at what one small town needed. Power. Roads. Water. And the people who live there.
A White House supply-chain review in twenty twenty-one, passing on industry comments, said that wafer-making inputs, including quartz crucibles, were sole-sourced, or not made in the United States.

The industry's answer, so far, has not been to leave. Sibelco had already announced an estimated two hundred million dollars to double its capacity here, and later put a possible second expansion at around five hundred million.

Others are trying to catch up. A Chinese producer's annual report lists a sixty-thousand-tonne-a-year project for high-purity quartz sand. And some bowl makers offer bowls lined inside with man-made silica.
And new chip factories keep rising, far from these mountains. India has approved twelve semiconductor units, including a fab at Dholera, in Gujarat.
The silicon fab among them will need wafers. And India's solar makers, the government says, still rely substantially on imported wafers. Behind a great many wafers stands a quartz bowl.
We tend to picture a chokepoint as a narrow sea, watched by warships.
This one is a green valley, two mining companies, and about two thousand people.
The most advanced machines on Earth begin in a bowl. And the world's leading source of its quartz, by the companies' own account, is here, in Spruce Pine.
